app.name: GitHub OAuth App (github.com developer OAuth apps)

verdict.summary: Registering a GitHub OAuth app is a short form on github.com with no review for normal use. The work is in the details: org owners may need to approve the app, and Composio's default scopes are much broader than most apps need. Marketplace publishing is the only path that involves review.
verdict.hands_on_effort: 30-60 min for registration and a test authorization; add time for org approval and scope reduction
verdict.time_to_first_connection: 15 min once you have a Composio callback URL
verdict.approval_wait: none for using your own OAuth app; Marketplace listing review is about 2-6 weeks (community-reported, no SLA)

gates.name: Your own account (developer use)
gates.unlocks: Create the OAuth app and connect your own GitHub account to it using your own client ID and secret.
limits: One user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps.
An app can register up to 10 callback URLs.
Only put public information in the app name, homepage and description.

gates.name: Invited and org users (no published GitHub review found)
gates.unlocks: Other GitHub accounts can authorize the app. Access into an organization depends on that org's OAuth app restrictions, and private or internal apps can only be signed into by members of the owning enterprise or org.
limits: Organizations with restrictions on: unapproved OAuth apps cannot access private org resources, and restrictions are on by default for new orgs.
Members can request org access for an unapproved app, and app access requests are enabled by default.
Private or internal OAuth apps can only be signed into by members of the owning enterprise or org.
Users can edit token scopes, so you may receive fewer scopes than requested.
Expiring tokens are opt-in: 8-hour access token and 6-month refresh token. New apps have it on by default.
Primary rate limit for an OAuth user token is the user's own 5,000 requests per hour.
GitHub publishes no install or user cap for unlisted OAuth apps.
gates.time_to_reach: Same day once Gate 1 works, plus any org owner approval needed

gates.name: Public use (no review for plain OAuth; review only for Marketplace listing)
gates.unlocks: Anyone can authorize a plain OAuth app. A GitHub Marketplace listing is optional and is the only step that goes through review.
limits: Marketplace listings need a privacy policy link, support link or email, a pricing plan, and publisher contact info.
Paid Marketplace plans for OAuth apps need at least 200 users and a verified publisher organization. A personal-account app must be transferred to an org first.
Paid listings must support monthly and annual billing.
Only organization owners can create and submit listings for org-owned apps.
No formal GitHub review for a plain OAuth app was found in the official pages reviewed.
gates.time_to_reach: No wait for plain OAuth use. Marketplace review about 2-6 weeks (community-reported).

steps.title: Decide whether a GitHub App fits better
steps.detail: GitHub recommends a GitHub App over an OAuth app because it uses fine-grained permissions and short-lived tokens. OAuth apps only act on behalf of a user and have lower rate limits. Continue with an OAuth app only if Composio's GitHub integration requires it, which it does for this guide.
gotchas: OAuth apps do not scale; rate limit increases are granted per app and apply to every token issued to it.

steps.title: Get the Composio callback URL
steps.detail: In your Composio project, open the auth config for GitHub and copy the callback URL shown there. Confirm it before you register it on GitHub, because the findings show two different Composio callback URLs.

values.label: Redirect URI
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

gotchas: The GitHub authorize endpoint accepts unknown client IDs at this step, so a wrong callback will only fail later with redirect_uri_mismatch.

steps.title: Open the GitHub developer settings
steps.detail: Sign in to GitHub and go to Settings, then Developer settings, then OAuth Apps. Use the personal account or an org where you have admin access.

steps.title: Register a new OAuth app
steps.detail: Click New OAuth App. Enter the Application name, the Homepage URL (required), and an optional Description. Keep only public information in these fields.

values.label: Homepage URL
values.value: Your public app or company URL

steps.title: Set the callback URL and token expiry
steps.detail: In Authorization callback URL, paste the Composio callback URL. Add a second callback only if you need one; the limit is 10. Tick Expire user access tokens if you want 8-hour access tokens with 6-month refresh tokens. New apps have this on by default.

values.label: Redirect URI
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

gotchas: Expiring tokens require your code to refresh them by exchanging the refresh token for a new pair.

steps.title: Register and copy credentials
steps.detail: Click Register application. Copy the Client ID shown after registration. Then generate a client secret on the app's settings page and store it in Composio's auth config, not in client-side code.

values.label: Client secret
values.value: Generated on the app settings page

gotchas: Never include the client secret in client-side code or on a user's device.

steps.title: Check organization OAuth restrictions
steps.detail: If the app will touch org repositories, check whether the org restricts OAuth apps. In an org with restrictions on, an unapproved app cannot reach private org resources until an org owner approves it. Ask the org owner to approve the app by its client ID before you test against org data.
gotchas: New organizations have restrictions on by default.
Members can submit an access request, and that request is enabled by default. Approval is a manual step by the org owner.

steps.title: Reduce requested scopes
steps.detail: Draft the scope list the app actually needs and a one-line justification for each scope. Remove the Composio defaults that the app does not use. Pass the scope string in the scope parameter of the authorize request, space-separated.

values.label: Composio default scopes
values.value: repo, user, gist, notifications, project, workflow, codespace

gotchas: repo and admin:org grant full access to repositories or organizations.
user already includes user:email, so requesting both stores only user.
Users can edit scopes, so handle a reduced scope set after authorization.

steps.title: Request offline_access for expiring tokens
steps.detail: If you enabled expiring tokens, add offline_access to the authorization request. This triggers the short-lived token pattern for that authorization and is the recommended way to test the rollout before changing the app registration.

steps.title: Turn off wildcard callback matching
steps.detail: Open the app's settings and review each callback URL. Disable wildcard matching on any URI you do not need it for. GitHub has asked developers to review this setting.
gotchas: Apps with a single redirect URI had wildcard matching on as a legacy default.

steps.title: Run a test authorization
steps.detail: From Composio, connect a GitHub account that is not the app owner and one that is an org member subject to org restrictions. Confirm the consent screen lists the scopes you expect and that a redirect_uri_mismatch error does not appear. Test both with and without offline_access.
gotchas: Watch for scopes being reduced by the user at consent.
Plan around rate limits: 5,000 requests per hour per user token, shared with that user's other tokens and apps.

steps.title: Decide on Marketplace listing
steps.detail: Skip this step for normal OAuth use. A Marketplace listing is only needed to publish the app on GitHub Marketplace. If you choose it, the app must do more than authentication and must be publicly available, and it needs a privacy policy, a support link or email, and a pricing plan.
gotchas: Paid plans need at least 200 users and a verified publisher organization. Personal-account apps must be transferred to an org first.
Only org owners can create and submit listings for org-owned apps.

steps.title: Submit a Marketplace listing (only if chosen)
steps.detail: Accept the Marketplace Developer Agreement and submit the listing. Monthly and annual billing must be supported for paid plans. After submission, an onboarding expert will contact you. Do not resubmit to speed things up.
gotchas: Community reports say resubmitting may restart review.
Check that 2FA is enabled and that your public email is verified before submitting.

steps.title: Wait for Marketplace review (only if submitted)
steps.detail: GitHub does not publish a review SLA. A community discussion reports about 2-6 weeks for review, with some taking longer. Plain OAuth use does not wait on this step.

requirements.detail: Register the Composio callback URL in Authorization callback URL. Host and port must match exactly; path must be a subdirectory of the registered callback.
Required on the registration form. Use only public information.
Store the secret in Composio's auth config; never in client-side code or on a user device.

requirements.item: Org owner approval for restricted orgs
requirements.detail: Orgs with OAuth app restrictions must approve the app before it can reach private org resources.
Marketplace listings need a valid privacy policy link. Not needed for plain OAuth use.
Paid Marketplace plans require a verified publisher organization and at least 200 users.

scopes.effect: Full access to repositories. Composio default. Request only if the app needs repo access; GitHub publishes no separate sensitive tier for OAuth apps, so no review is tied to it.
Includes user:email and user:follow. Requesting user together with user:email stores only user.
Gist access. Composio default; drop if unused.
Notification access. Composio default; drop if unused.
Project access. Composio default; drop if unused.
Lets the app update GitHub Actions workflows. Composio default; request only if needed.
Codespace access. Composio default; drop if unused.
Full management of an organization and its teams, projects and memberships. Avoid unless required.
Permits deleting repositories. Avoid unless required.
Triggers the short-lived (8-hour access, 6-month refresh) token pattern for an authorization.

blockers.symptom: Members of an org see an access request or cannot reach private org repositories with the new app.
blockers.cause: The org restricts OAuth apps, and the app has not been approved by an org owner.
blockers.fix: An org owner approves the app in the org's OAuth app settings. Test first on a personal account if approval is slow.

blockers.symptom: Outside users cannot sign in to a private or internal OAuth app.
blockers.cause: Since the June 2025 change, a private or internal OAuth app can only be signed into by members of the owning enterprise or organization.
blockers.fix: Use a public OAuth app for outside testers, or limit testing to members of the owning org or enterprise.

blockers.symptom: Paid Marketplace listing is rejected or blocked for a personal-account app.
blockers.cause: Paid plans require at least 200 users and an app owned by a verified publisher organization.
blockers.fix: Transfer the app to a verified publisher org before creating a paid plan, or keep the listing free or unlisted.

blockers.cause: The callback URL registered on GitHub does not exactly match the redirect URI that Composio sends.
blockers.fix: Copy the callback URL from the Composio auth config exactly and paste it as the GitHub callback URL. Check which Composio callback your project uses before saving.

composio.note: Start on Composio's managed GitHub OAuth app to prototype. Register your own OAuth app when you need your own client ID and secret, your own callback URL, a branded consent screen, or separate rate limits. Self-registered apps should request only the scopes they need, not Composio's broad default set. Confirm the Composio callback URL before registering it on GitHub.

evidence.claim: OAuth apps are created from the user's Developer settings page under OAuth apps, via the New OAuth App button, under a personal account or any org where the user has admin access.
evidence.quote: You can create and register an OAuth app under your personal account or under any organization you have administrative access to.

evidence.claim: Since the June 2025 change, a private OAuth app or one owned by an Enterprise Managed User account can only be signed into by members of the owning enterprise or organization, which affects testing an internal or private app with outside users.
evidence.quote: users must now be a member of the enterprise if it is internal, or the owning organization if it's private.

evidence.claim: Since Aug 14, 2026 OAuth apps can opt into expiring tokens: an 8-hour access token and a 6-month refresh token, refreshed by exchanging the refresh token for a new pair; new apps have this enabled by default.
evidence.quote: If an app opts in, they get an access token that lives for eight hours and a refresh token that's valid for six months.

evidence.claim: Requesting the offline_access scope triggers the short-lived token pattern for an individual authorization, and it is the recommended way to test the rollout before changing the app registration.
evidence.quote: Include the offline_access scope in their authentication request, which triggers the short-lived token pattern.

evidence.claim: Redirect/callback rules: redirect_uri is optional; when given, its host (excluding subdomains) and port must exactly match a registered callback, and its path must be a subdirectory of it. Without redirect_uri GitHub uses the first registered callback.
evidence.quote: If left out, GitHub will redirect users to the first callback URL configured in the OAuth app settings.

evidence.claim: Wildcard matching for callbacks is an opt-in per-URI setting; apps with a single redirect URI had wildcard matching enabled as a legacy behavior, and the 2026 changelog asks developers to disable it if not needed.
evidence.quote: Please review your apps and disable wildcard matching if you do not need it.

evidence.claim: Scopes are declared in the authorize request as a space-separated list (scope parameter), and the authorization form shows the requested scopes to the user; scopes limit a token and grant nothing beyond what the user already has.
evidence.quote: Your OAuth app can request the scopes in the initial authorization request.

evidence.claim: The full scope catalog is documented, including repo, user (includes user:email and user:follow), gist, notifications, project, workflow, codespace, admin:org, admin:repo_hook, delete_repo, and offline_access. Broad scopes like repo and admin:org grant full access to repos or organizations; GitHub publishes no separate sensitive or restricted scope tier for OAuth apps on this page.
evidence.quote: Fully manage the organization and its teams, projects, and memberships.

evidence.claim: Users can edit token scopes after authorization, so an app receives less access than requested in some cases and must handle a reduced scope set.
evidence.quote: users can edit their scopes, effectively granting your application less access than you originally requested.

evidence.claim: Scopes are normalized: requesting user together with user:email stores only user, because user already includes user:email.

Authorize endpoint probe: https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize is live. With a made-up client_id and the Composio callback, GitHub returned a 302 to a sign-in page, with no OAuth error parameter, so the endpoint does not reject unknown client IDs at the authorize step.

Registration form fields: application name, homepage URL (required), optional description, authorization callback URL(s), optional device flow toggle, and an 'Expire user access tokens' checkbox; the form ends with a Register application button.
Developer settings page probe: https://github.com/settings/developers redirects to a GitHub sign-in wall for an anonymous visitor, so the portal exists and requires login.
Scopes documentation page probe returned HTTP 200 without a login wall.

Marketplace listing (only needed for publishing to GitHub Marketplace, not for OAuth use): all listings need valid publisher contact info, a relevant description, a pricing plan, a valid privacy policy link, a support link or email, and working extra links; the app must do more than authentication and must be publicly available.
evidence.quote: Listings must have a valid link to a privacy policy.

evidence.claim: Marketplace listings also require the Marketplace Developer Agreement to be accepted at submission, and only organization owners can create and submit listings for organization-owned apps; the GitHub App manager role does not grant listing permission.
evidence.quote: For organization-owned apps, only organization owners can create and submit listings in GitHub Marketplace.

evidence.claim: Paid Marketplace plans for OAuth apps require at least 200 users, and paid plans require the app to be owned by a verified publisher organization; a personal-account app must first be transferred to an org.
evidence.quote: OAuth apps should have a minimum of 200 users.

evidence.claim: Paid listing must also support monthly and annual billing and handle purchase events for new purchases, upgrades, downgrades, cancellations and free trials.
evidence.quote: Apps must support both monthly and annual billing for paid subscriptions purchases.

evidence.claim: Marketplace review timing is not published by GitHub; a community discussion reports a typical wait of about 2–6 weeks for review and notes there is no official SLA.
evidence.quote: the typical review time is 2–6 weeks, but some cases may take longer.

evidence.claim: Submitting for review (Marketplace): after submission an onboarding expert contacts the publisher with more onboarding information; the listing status shows as under review with email notifications.
evidence.quote: After you submit your app for review, an onboarding expert will contact you with additional information about the onboarding process.

evidence.claim: Community reports that a Marketplace submission is not restarted by resubmitting, but the reply advises against resubmitting because it may restart review, and advises checking that 2FA is enabled and the public email is verified.
evidence.quote: Submitting again may restart the review process.

evidence.claim: Publisher verification: Marketplace paid listings require a verified publisher organization; the docs page on applying for it is listed in the Marketplace docs.
evidence.quote: your app must be owned by an organization that is a verified publisher.

evidence.claim: A single user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps.
Primary rate limit for an OAuth user token is the user's own limit of 5,000 requests per hour, shared with other apps and personal tokens that user uses.
evidence.quote: Primary rate limits for OAuth access tokens generated by a OAuth app are dictated by the primary rate limits for authenticated users.

evidence.claim: OAuth apps can also call public endpoints with client ID and secret at 5,000 requests per hour per app, or 15,000 for apps owned by a GitHub Enterprise Cloud org.
evidence.quote: For these requests, the rate limit is 5,000 requests per hour per OAuth app.

evidence.claim: Token issuance is separately rate-limited: GitHub Enterprise Server 3.14 docs state OAuth apps are limited to 2,000 access token requests per hour, and above that new token generation is temporarily blocked (version-specific; verify on github.com docs).
evidence.quote: OAuth apps are subject to a rate limit of 2,000 access token requests per hour.

evidence.claim: Redirect/callback configuration must match exactly; a mismatch returns redirect_uri_mismatch with the message that the redirect_uri must match the registered callback URL.
evidence.quote: The redirect_uri MUST match the registered callback URL for this application.

evidence.claim: Credentials: the client ID is shown once registration succeeds, and the client secret is generated on the app's settings page; the client secret must never go into client-side code.
evidence.quote: Never include your app's client secret in client-side code or in code that runs on a user device.

evidence.claim: Organization-owned OAuth apps: the app can be registered under an organization where the user is admin, and the Developer settings path is the same for org apps.
No separate PKCE, refresh token setting, or install cap for unreviewed OAuth apps was found on GitHub's official pages reviewed.
An OAuth app can register up to 10 callback URLs, added with an Add callback URL control.
evidence.quote: You can enter up to 10 callback URLs.

evidence.claim: Warning from GitHub: only put information you consider public in the app name, homepage and description; avoid sensitive data such as internal URLs.
GitHub recommends building a GitHub App instead of an OAuth app, noting that GitHub Apps use fine-grained permissions and short-lived tokens while OAuth apps only act on behalf of a user.
evidence.quote: Consider building a GitHub App instead of an OAuth app.

evidence.claim: OAuth apps have lower rate limits than GitHub Apps and do not scale; rate limit increases for OAuth apps are granted per app and apply to every token issued to that app.
evidence.quote: OAuth apps have lower rate limits and do not scale.

evidence.claim: Organizations can restrict OAuth apps: when restrictions are on, unapproved OAuth apps cannot access private organization resources or send hook deliveries from private repos, and enabling restrictions is the default for newly created organizations.
evidence.quote: When you create a new organization, OAuth app access restrictions are enabled by default.

evidence.claim: When a member or outside collaborator tries to use an unapproved OAuth app in an org, the request goes to the org; members and outside collaborators can request organization access for unapproved apps, and this request is enabled by default.
evidence.quote: By default, app access requests are enabled.

open_questions: Composio callback URL discrepancy: the Composio toolkit record lists https://backend.composio.dev/api/v1/auth-apps/add as the default redirect URI, but the authorize probe used https://backend.composio.dev/api/v3/toolkits/auth/callback. Confirm which one your Composio project uses before registering it on GitHub.
No GitHub-documented cap on how many users can authorize an unreviewed or unlisted OAuth app was found. The 'install limit' does not appear to be a published number.
Whether GitHub supports PKCE for OAuth apps was not confirmed.
The GitHub OAuth/OIDC discovery document was linked but not fetched or probed.
The 2,000 access-token-request limit is from a GitHub Enterprise Server 3.14 page; the current github.com value was not confirmed.
Whether a plain OAuth app needs any formal GitHub review was not found; the findings suggest none, but this is inferred from missing evidence.
Marketplace review timing (2-6 weeks) is community-reported only; no SLA was found.
GitHub does not appear to publish a sensitive or restricted scope tier for OAuth apps, so scope tiers are marked unknown.
Whether the expiring-token default applies to apps created before Aug 14, 2026 was not established; the findings only say new apps have it on by default.
